abstract: Adaptation of neuronal network activity is critical for maintaining brain homeostasis and coping with changing computational demands. Microglia, the brain's innate immune cells, are increasingly recognized to shape neuronal function in the healthy brain, yet their contribution to inhibitory circuit dynamics and network synchronization remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that microglia establish a closed-loop feedback circuit that regulates synchronized network activity in the gamma frequency range, a key feature of cognitive processes that critically depends on fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVIs). This mechanism operates in ex vivo mouse hippocampal and human neocortical circuits, indicating conservation across brain regions and species. During gamma oscillations, microglia preferentially recruit their processes to PVI somata through P2Y12 receptor-dependent purinergic signaling, whereas comparable targeting is absent around pyramidal neurons. Blockade of P2Y12 enhances gamma power, as does inhibition of interleukin-1 receptor type 1 (IL-1R1), an effect absent in P2Y12-deficient mice. P2Y12-IL-1R1 signaling functionally converges on adenosine A1 receptor activation, consistent with an IL-1{beta}-adenosine-mediated neuroimmune feedback mechanism. At the cellular level, adenosine reduces excitatory synaptic input onto PVIs, whereas IL-1{beta} attenuates their fast-spiking behavior. Together, our findings establish microglia as physiological regulators of inhibitory network synchronization, linking preferential interactions with PVIs to P2Y12-coupled cytokine signaling and homeostatic gain control of gamma oscillations.
